You handed over keys on 31 Aug 2026 and the landlord is holding ₹25,000 without showing any bills. From what you've told me, the main conditions for getting your money back seem to be met — you have a registered agreement and bank-transfer proof. The landlord's claim of 'general damage' without bills is a weak spot on his side.

**Your options (cheapest → formal):**

1. **Written demand** (WhatsApp/email) — state the amount, ask for bills, give a deadline. Free, same day.
2. **Legal notice** demanding refund within ~15 days. You can send it yourself; a lawyer's letter carries more weight. Cost: a few hundred to a couple of thousand for drafting.
3. **Free Lok Adalat / legal aid** via District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) or call **NALSA 15100** (toll-free). No court fee, settlement-focused.

citations.title: 3 years to sue for compensation for breach of contract
citations.plain: A suit for compensation for breach of a contract (written or implied), where no other article covers it specifically, must be filed within 3 years. Time runs from the date of the breach. If there are repeated breaches, it runs from the breach you sue on; if the breach is continuing, from when it stops.

citations.title: Summary suits for fixed money claims
citations.plain: A summary suit is a faster procedure for clear money claims. It covers suits on cheques, bills of exchange, hundis and promissory notes, and suits to recover a fixed debt or 'liquidated' amount (with or without interest) arising from a written contract, a law that fixes the sum, or a guarantee. The defendant may defend only with the court's permission ('leave to defend'). It is available only in courts where the Order applies.

citations.title: Pre-litigation settlement through Lok Adalat
citations.plain: Even before filing a case, one party can apply to the District or State Legal Services Authority to have a civil dispute, or a compoundable criminal matter, referred to a Lok Adalat for amicable settlement. Non-compoundable offences are excluded. This is available now, unlike Mediation Act section 5.

citations.title: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100
citations.plain: Call the national legal aid helpline 15100 (toll-free) for free legal advice and help applying for legal aid. You can also apply for legal aid or victim compensation online via the NALSA website.

citations.title: Compensation for breach of contract
citations.plain: If someone breaks a contract with you, you can claim money for the loss it caused. The loss must be one that naturally follows from the breach, or one both sides knew was likely when they made the contract. Remote or indirect losses are not covered. This is the basis for claiming back an unpaid deposit, rent or salary owed under a contract.

citations.title: States that revised tenancy laws on MTA lines (as of July 2022)
citations.plain: As of July 2022, the Housing Ministry reported that Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and Assam had revised their tenancy laws along the lines of the Model Tenancy Act. Other states continue under their own rent control laws, so the deposit cap and the rent authority procedure vary by state.

LEGAL NOTICE

By Registered Post A.D. / Speed Post

Date: [[FILL: date]]

From:
[[FILL: Your Full Name]]
[[FILL: Your Current Address]]
[[FILL: Your Phone Number]]

To:
Mr. Ramesh Gowda
[[FILL: Landlord's Full Address]]

Subject: Notice for refund of security deposit regarding the premises at [[FILL: Address of the rented flat]].

Dear Sir,

1. I am writing to you regarding the tenancy of the premises located at [[FILL: Address of the rented flat]], which I vacated on 31 August 2026.

2. As per our registered rent agreement, I had paid a security deposit of ₹60,000 (Rupees Sixty Thousand only) to you via bank transfer.

3. On 31 August 2026, I handed over the peaceful possession of the premises and the keys to you. At that time, the property was in good condition, consistent with normal wear and tear.

4. It has been over two months since I vacated the premises. You have informed me of your intention to deduct ₹25,000 from the deposit for painting and general damage. However, you have failed to provide any invoices, bills, or proof of expenditure to justify these deductions.

5. Under Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, you are obligated to return the security deposit upon the termination of the tenancy, subject only to legitimate deductions for actual damages, which must be substantiated.

6. I hereby demand that you refund the balance amount of ₹35,000 (Rupees Thirty-Five Thousand only) to me within 15 days of the receipt of this notice. Please transfer the amount to the following bank account:
   Bank Name: [[FILL: Your Bank Name]]
   Account Holder Name: [[FILL: Your Name]]
   Account Number: [[FILL: Your Account Number]]
   IFSC Code: [[FILL: Your IFSC Code]]

7. If you fail to comply with this demand within the stipulated period, I shall be constrained to initiate appropriate legal proceedings against you for recovery of the amount, including interest and legal costs, by approaching the competent court or the relevant legal forum.

Copy retained for record.

Sincerely,

[[FILL: Your Name]]
[[FILL: Your Phone Number]]
[[FILL: Your Email Address]]

send_instructions: Print two copies of this notice. Sign both copies.
Send one copy to Mr. Ramesh Gowda via 'Registered Post A.D.' (Acknowledgement Due) or 'Speed Post' from your nearest post office. This provides you with a tracking number and proof of delivery.
Keep the second copy and the original postal receipt safely with your records.
If you receive the 'Acknowledgement Due' card back in the mail, staple it to your copy of the notice as proof that he received it.
If he does not pay within 15 days of receiving the notice, you may consider filing a civil suit for recovery or approaching the local District Legal Services Authority for mediation/Lok Adalat.
You can contact the NALSA helpline at 15100 for further guidance on how to proceed if the landlord continues to withhold your money.
